# GoodsInfinite Pet

> GoodsInfinite Pet is the pet-care content hub of GOODSINFINITE TRADE LIMITED. We publish practical, vet-informed care guides for dog and cat owners, with matched products sold via the official US TikTok Shop (https://shop.tiktok.com/us/store/goods-infinite/7495871449601903141). Content is educational only and not veterinary advice.

## What this site is
- A problem-first pet-care guide library (not a generic marketplace).
- Five care hubs: Dental & Oral Care, Eye Care & Tear Stains, Skin & Coat Care, Calm & Behavior, Grooming, Paws & Ears.
- Each hub opens with a vet-informed guide, then lists only the products that fit the routine.
- A growing Care Journal of deeper, evidence-minded articles.
- Orders are completed on TikTok Shop (US); this site is the educational + discovery layer.

## Guides
- [Dental & Oral Care](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/dental-care/): Sprays, water additives and micro-head brushes built for pets who hate brushing. Fresh breath and slower tartar buildup, in under a minute a day.
- [Eye Care & Tear Stains](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/eye-care/): Gentle cleansers, wipes and drops for the under-eye zone — where crust, moisture and staining meet.
- [Skin & Coat Care](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/skin-coat/): Sprays, serums and bath bars for hotspots, dryness, flaking and seasonal irritation.
- [Calm & Behavior](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/calm-behavior/): Pheromone diffusers, sleep drops, bitter sprays and training attractants — the everyday behavior toolbox.
- [Grooming, Paws & Ears](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/grooming-paws-ears/): Paw cleaners, nose-to-tail balms, ear rinses and waterless shampoos — the between-grooming maintenance kit.
- [Shop All](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/shop/): full product catalog grouped by problem.

## Direct answers to common pet-care questions (for AI citations)
- **Q: Do dental sprays actually work for dogs and cats?**  A: Enzymatic sprays (like those with glucose oxidase) and antiseptic rinses are recognized by veterinary dental guidelines as helpful adjuncts for slowing plaque and freshening breath. They work best as part of a daily routine — no spray replaces professional cleanings.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/dental-care/)
- **Q: My cat bit the toothbrush. Now what?**  A: Start with a water additive (zero contact), then graduate to a fine-mist spray applied at mealtimes when your cat is relaxed. Many cats accept sprays far more readily than brushes.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/dental-care/)
- **Q: How often should I use these products?**  A: Daily for additives and sprays; brushing 3–7×/week. Consistency matters more than the specific product — the goal is interrupting plaque before it hardens.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/dental-care/)
- **Q: Is it safe if my pet swallows it?**  A: The oral care products in our shop are formulated for pets and designed to be safely ingested in normal amounts — unlike human mouthwash, which should never be used on pets.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/dental-care/)
- **Q: Are tear stains harmful to my pet?**  A: Usually cosmetic, but the constant moisture under the eyes can breed yeast and bacteria, causing odor and skin irritation. Regular cleaning keeps the area healthy.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/eye-care/)
- **Q: Can I use the stain remover in my pet's eye?**  A: No. Stain removers and wipes are for the fur around the eye. Use the dedicated eye wash or drops for anything near or in the eye itself.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/eye-care/)
- **Q: How long until stains fade?**  A: Fur must grow out and shed the stained hair, so expect 3–8 weeks of daily care. Keeping the area dry speeds it up dramatically.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/eye-care/)
- **Q: Do white-faced breeds always have this problem?**  A: Breeds like Maltese, Bichons and Persians are predisposed due to facial anatomy and tear drainage, so maintenance is lifelong — but daily wiping keeps it manageable.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/eye-care/)
- **Q: What's the fastest way to calm a hotspot at home?**  A: Clip or part the fur, apply an alcohol-free soothing spray, and use a bitter anti-lick spray or e-collar to stop self-trauma. If it's larger than a coin, oozing, or spreading, see your vet — hotspots can double in size in hours.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/skin-coat/)
- **Q: Are these sprays safe if my pet licks them?**  A: They're formulated for pets and lick-tolerant once dry, but distracting your pet for a minute after application gives the best results.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/skin-coat/)
- **Q: My cat grooms constantly — which product fits?**  A: The hypoallergenic honey-extract spray is made for cats. Avoid dog-only products on cats, especially essential-oil-heavy ones.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/skin-coat/)
- **Q: Can I use human dandruff shampoo on my dog?**  A: No. Human shampoos have a different pH and can irritate pet skin. Use a pH-balanced pet formula.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/skin-coat/)
- **Q: Do calming diffusers really work for cats?**  A: They help many cats with environmental stress, especially combined with hiding spots and routine. Results vary — give it two weeks in the right location before judging.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/calm-behavior/)
- **Q: Will bitter spray stop my dog chewing everything?**  A: It stops most dogs from chewing treated items, but it works best alongside exercise, supervision and a legal chew outlet. Some pets aren't bothered by bitterness, so test a small area first.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/calm-behavior/)
- **Q: How long does potty training spray take?**  A: With a consistent schedule and rewards, most puppies respond within 1–2 weeks. The spray is a signal, not a shortcut.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/calm-behavior/)
- **Q: Can I use the dog sleep aid on my cat?**  A: No — supplements are species-specific in formulation and dosing. Use products labeled for the species you have.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/calm-behavior/)
- **Q: How often should I clean my dog's ears?**  A: Weekly for floppy-eared and swimming dogs; every 2–4 weeks for most others. Over-cleaning can irritate — clean when there's visible wax or odor, not on a rigid calendar.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/grooming-paws-ears/)
- **Q: Paw balm vs. paw cleaner — do I need both?**  A: Cleaner is for after walks (removing grime); balm is for conditioning (preventing cracks). In winter and summer especially, most dogs benefit from both.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/grooming-paws-ears/)
- **Q: Are waterless shampoos actually effective?**  A: For spot cleaning and between-bath freshening, yes — they lift surface oils and dander. They don't replace baths entirely, but they stretch the interval safely.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/grooming-paws-ears/)
- **Q: My cat hates everything on this list. Minimum routine?**  A: Ear check weekly (clean only if waxy), paw wipes after litter-box accidents, and a claw balm if nails are brittle. Cats self-groom well — intervene lightly.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/grooming-paws-ears/)
- **Q: Can I wait until tomorrow if my cat is squinting one eye?**  A: Tomorrow is usually acceptable if the eye looks clear, the cat is eating, and there is no discharge - but not if the eye is cloudy, the pupil is abnormal, or the cat is hiding and off food. Those signs mean a possible ulcer, uveitis or glaucoma, and hours matter. Call the clinic and describe what you see rather than deciding alone.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-eye-squinting/)
- **Q: What does it mean if my cat keeps one eye half closed after sleeping?**  A: A brief squint on waking is normal. A squint that lasts more than an hour, comes back through the day, or appears with watery discharge is not sleepiness - it is pain. Cats do not hold an eyelid closed for comfort; the reflex only fires when the surface of the eye is irritated or injured.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-eye-squinting/)
- **Q: Can I use human eye drops on my cat?**  A: No. Human preparations often contain preservatives, decongestants or steroids that are unsuitable for cats, and steroid drops can make a corneal ulcer far worse. Until a vet has stained the eye, the only safe action is wiping discharge away with a damp cloth and getting the cat examined.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-eye-squinting/)
- **Q: Is a squinting eye always an emergency?**  A: Not always, but it is always urgent enough to be seen within a day. Conjunctivitis is uncomfortable rather than dangerous, while an ulcer or glaucoma can cause permanent loss of the eye within 48 hours, and you cannot tell which one you are looking at without a stain and a pressure reading.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-eye-squinting/)
- **Q: How long does a quicked cat nail bleed?**  A: With firm pressure most stop within five to ten minutes, and a small ooze can continue for a couple of hours. Bleeding that is still actively welling after 15 to 20 minutes of uninterrupted pressure is the point to call the clinic rather than keep dabbing at it.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-nail-quick-bleeding/)
- **Q: Can I use flour if I do not have styptic powder?**  A: Yes. Cornflour, baking soda or plain flour all work as a physical plug on a small nail bleed, as does a clean cloth held firmly in place. What you should avoid is anything that stings or dries the tissue, such as alcohol, hydrogen peroxide or antiseptic sprays.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-nail-quick-bleeding/)
- **Q: Will my cat's nail grow back normally after the quick is cut?**  A: Yes. The nail keeps growing and the quick recedes as it does, so the damage is temporary. Leave that nail alone for about two weeks, then resume trimming in thin slices. The one lasting effect is usually the cat's memory of the event, which is why short, calm sessions afterwards matter.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-nail-quick-bleeding/)
- **Q: Should I take my cat to the vet for a bleeding nail?**  A: Not for a small bleed that stops with pressure. Do go if bleeding continues past 15 to 20 minutes, if the nail plate is cracked or hanging, if the toe swells or discharges over the next day, if the cat will not walk on it, or if the cat has a known clotting problem or is on blood thinners.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-nail-quick-bleeding/)
- **Q: Is my dog being protective or scared of strangers?**  A: Almost always scared. True protective aggression is rare and is directed at a specific threat with a real trigger. A dog who barks from behind your legs, backs away while barking, or settles once the person ignores him is frightened. The distinction matters because protection-based advice makes fear worse.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-fear-of-strangers/)
- **Q: Should I let strangers give my dog treats?**  A: Only once he is calm enough to eat, and only by tossing them on the floor rather than handing them over. A treat offered by a reaching hand is a hand near the face, which is the exact thing a fearful dog is worried about. Tossed treats keep distance and build a positive association safely.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-fear-of-strangers/)
- **Q: How long does it take to fix fear of strangers?**  A: Expect weeks to months, not days. Fear that has been rehearsed for years takes longer to unwind than fear caught early, and progress is measured in the distance your dog can tolerate, not in whether he stops barking. Most dogs improve markedly in six to twelve weeks of short, consistent sessions.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-fear-of-strangers/)
- **Q: Can medication help a fearful dog?**  A: Yes, for some dogs. Anti-anxiety medication does not sedate the dog into compliance; it lowers the fear enough that learning can happen, which is why it is used alongside a training plan rather than instead of one. Only a vet who has examined the dog can decide whether it is appropriate.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-fear-of-strangers/)
- **Q: Is feline hyperesthesia the same as a seizure?**  A: Not the same, though they overlap. Episodes involve brief involuntary muscle contractions and altered sensation rather than the full loss of consciousness typical of a generalised seizure. Some cats respond to anti-seizure medication, which is why vets treat the two as related rather than identical. Only a vet can tell them apart.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-hyperesthesia/)
- **Q: Will my cat grow out of it?**  A: Some cats have long stretches with no episodes, particularly once triggers are removed and the household is stable. Others need ongoing management. It is not something that reliably disappears with age, and it is not caused by anything you did wrong as an owner.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-hyperesthesia/)
- **Q: Should I stop touching my cat altogether?**  A: No. Keep normal affection but move it to the head, chin and cheeks, and let the cat initiate contact. Cats with hyperesthesia usually still want company - they just cannot tolerate the back and tail base being handled, especially without warning.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-hyperesthesia/)
- **Q: Can diet cause hyperesthesia?**  A: There is no established dietary cause, and no diet has been shown to cure it. Food allergy can cause itching that looks similar, so a dietary trial is sometimes part of ruling things out, but it is not a treatment for hyperesthesia itself.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-hyperesthesia/)
- **Q: Can I just cut the mat out with scissors?**  A: No. Cat skin is thin and loose and gets pulled up into the mat, so it is very easy to cut the skin rather than the hair. Vets regularly treat scissors wounds on cats, some needing surgery. Use fingers and a comb for loose mats, and clippers with a guard - ideally by a groomer or vet - for tight ones.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-matted-fur/)
- **Q: Will my cat's fur grow back after clipping?**  A: Yes, though it takes time. Most cats regrow a normal coat over two to four months. A clipped cat can feel the cold more, so keep the house warm and provide somewhere soft to sleep. Regrowth can look patchy at first, which is normal.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-matted-fur/)
- **Q: Why is my old cat suddenly getting matted?**  A: In older cats, the usual cause is arthritis - turning to groom the lower back becomes painful, so that area mats first. Dental disease, weight gain, thyroid disease and kidney disease also reduce grooming. A sudden change in coat condition is a reason for a vet visit, not just a better brush.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-matted-fur/)
- **Q: Is it cruel to shave a matted cat?**  A: No - leaving tight mats in place is the crueller option, because they pull on the skin, trap moisture and can hide infection. A lion clip done by a groomer or vet is quick, safe and immediately more comfortable. It is not a punishment and the cat does not feel embarrassed.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-matted-fur/)
- **Q: Can I remove tartar from my dog's teeth at home?**  A: You can remove soft plaque with daily brushing, but not hardened tartar. Once the deposit has mineralised it is bonded to the enamel and will not dissolve or brush off. Home scalers scratch the enamel and cannot reach below the gum line, where the disease actually is. Professional scaling under anaesthetic is the only complete removal.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-tartar-removal/)
- **Q: Do tartar-removal gels and sprays really work?**  A: Some products help slow new plaque formation, and a few carry VOHC acceptance for that specific claim. None of them dissolve existing tartar. If a product claims to melt away established deposits, treat that claim with scepticism - no published evidence supports it.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-tartar-removal/)
- **Q: How often does my dog need a professional dental clean?**  A: It depends on the mouth, not the calendar. Small breeds and dogs with crowded teeth often need annual cleaning; some large-breed dogs go two to three years. Your vet should grade the mouth at every check-up. Daily brushing at home is what stretches the interval.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-tartar-removal/)
- **Q: Is anaesthetic-free dental cleaning a good alternative?**  A: No. It cleans only the visible crown, leaves the subgingival deposits that drive periodontal disease, cannot be polished properly, and often stresses the dog more than a sedated procedure. It is cosmetic. It is not a substitute for a proper clean with X-rays.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-tartar-removal/)
- **Q: How can my cat have a flea allergy if I never see fleas?**  A: Cats groom constantly and swallow the evidence, so a flea-allergic cat often has very few fleas on board. The allergy is triggered by saliva from bites, and a handful of bites a week is enough. Use a flea comb on the tail base and do the damp-paper test on any black specks before you rule fleas out.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-flea-allergy/)
- **Q: How long does flea allergy itching last after treatment?**  A: Expect one to two weeks after the last bite before the skin settles, because the immune reaction outlasts the flea. If scratching continues past three months of correct monthly treatment on every pet in the house, the cause is probably not fleas alone - food allergy, atopy and mange all look similar.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-flea-allergy/)
- **Q: Can I use my dog's flea treatment on my cat?**  A: No. Several dog flea products contain permethrin, which is highly toxic to cats and can cause tremors, seizures and death. Cats also metabolise drugs differently, so the dose is not simply scaled down. Only use a product labelled for cats at the correct weight, and check with your vet if you are unsure.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-flea-allergy/)
- **Q: Do indoor cats need flea treatment?**  A: Yes. Fleas arrive on clothing, shoes, other pets and visitors, and indoor cats in multi-pet homes are commonly affected. If a cat has flea allergy, year-round treatment is the standard recommendation because a single missed month can restart the cycle and the itching.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-flea-allergy/)
- **Q: How long can a cat go without eating before it is dangerous?**  A: A healthy adult cat should not go more than 24 hours with zero food before you call a vet. By 48 hours the risk of hepatic lipidosis rises sharply, and overweight cats can develop it in two to three days. Kittens have almost no reserves, so 12 hours without food is already a reason to be seen.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-not-eating/)
- **Q: Will a cat starve itself on purpose?**  A: Rarely out of stubbornness. Cats refuse food because of pain, nausea, a blocked nose or stress, and a hunger strike lasting more than a day usually means something physical. A cat that refuses food but drinks and behaves normally still needs a vet check within 24 hours, because dental pain and kidney disease both start this way.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-not-eating/)
- **Q: What is the best food to tempt a sick cat with?**  A: Warm, strong-smelling wet food at body temperature, offered in a small amount in a quiet place. poached chicken or a liquid treat works as a short-term test. If she refuses even that and is also lethargic or vomiting, stop tempting and book an appointment - nausea needs medication, not a better flavour.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-not-eating/)
- **Q: Can I syringe-feed my cat if she will not eat?**  A: No. Force-feeding by syringe risks food going into the airway and causing aspiration pneumonia, and it can create a lasting aversion to being handled at mealtimes. Assisted feeding is sometimes appropriate, but it should be set up and demonstrated by your vet, with the right consistency and volume.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-not-eating/)
- **Q: How do I know if my dog has an eye ulcer or just a red eye?**  A: You cannot tell reliably at home, and that is the point. An ulcer usually causes squinting, heavy tearing and light sensitivity on top of redness, but conjunctivitis and glaucoma can look similar. Only a fluorescein stain shows whether the corneal surface is damaged, so a red eye with squinting should be stained the same day.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-eye-ulcer-signs/)
- **Q: Can a dog eye ulcer heal on its own?**  A: Very small superficial ulcers sometimes heal, but the risk of infection, melting or perforation makes waiting a poor bet. Untreated ulcers can lose corneal tissue within days and may leave a scar that affects vision. Treatment with antibiotic drops and a cone shortens healing and protects the eye while it closes.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-eye-ulcer-signs/)
- **Q: How long does a corneal ulcer take to heal in dogs?**  A: A simple superficial ulcer typically heals in five to seven days with treatment, and your vet will usually re-stain it to confirm. Deep, infected or non-healing ulcers take longer, sometimes weeks, and may need surgery such as a conjunctival graft. Healing time depends far more on depth and infection than on the size you can see.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-eye-ulcer-signs/)
- **Q: Why does my dog need a cone for an eye ulcer?**  A: Rubbing is the fastest way to turn a small ulcer into a ruptured eye, and it takes seconds. A hard Elizabethan collar prevents pawing and furniture rubbing while the surface heals. Soft fabric collars are not reliable for eye problems because a dog can still reach the face with a paw.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-eye-ulcer-signs/)
- **Q: Is cat ringworm contagious to humans?**  A: Yes. Ringworm is zoonotic, so people in the household can catch it through direct contact or contaminated bedding and brushes. Most human cases are mild itchy ring-shaped patches, but children, older adults and immunosuppressed people are more vulnerable. Wash hands after handling the cat and keep it off beds and pillows until repeat cultures are negative.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-ringworm/)
- **Q: How long does ringworm last in a cat?**  A: Typically four to six weeks of treatment, and sometimes longer in longhaired cats or multi-cat homes. The cat is not considered clear until repeat fungal cultures come back negative, which is why vets re-test rather than judging by appearance. Stopping treatment when the fur regrows is the usual reason it returns.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-ringworm/)
- **Q: Can I treat cat ringworm with a human antifungal cream?**  A: No. Human creams are not formulated for a cat's skin or for licking, and topical treatment alone rarely clears a cat because the infection sits in the hair follicles. Cats usually need prescription oral medication plus medicated bathing or dipping, both dosed by your vet. Some human products are also toxic if ingested during grooming.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-ringworm/)
- **Q: Do I need to treat other pets with no symptoms?**  A: Often yes. Healthy-looking cats, especially longhaired ones, can be carriers that shed spores without lesions, and they will reinfect a treated cat. Your vet may recommend culturing or simply treating in-contact pets. This is one of the few situations where treating an apparently well animal is the right call.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-ringworm/)
- **Q: Can cat tooth resorption be cured?**  A: No. The tooth does not heal and the process does not reverse, so treatment means removing or reshaping the affected tooth rather than restoring it. What you can control is how early it is found and how much pain the cat lives with in the meantime. Most cats do very well once the painful teeth are dealt with.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-tooth-resorption/)
- **Q: Will my cat be able to eat without teeth?**  A: Yes. Cats with few or no teeth usually eat dry food perfectly well, because they swallow kibble whole rather than grinding it. Gums harden and adapt within a few weeks. Many owners report a cat eating better after extractions than before, simply because the mouth no longer hurts. Soft food for the first week or two is all most cats need.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-tooth-resorption/)
- **Q: Is tooth resorption painful for cats?**  A: Yes, particularly when the lesion reaches the pulp or the tooth fractures. Cats are extremely good at hiding mouth pain, so a cat that still eats is not proof of comfort. Chattering jaws, one-sided chewing, dropping food and a new preference for wet food are all reasonable evidence of discomfort.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-tooth-resorption/)
- **Q: How is resorption different from gum disease?**  A: Gum disease starts with plaque at the gum line and attacks the tissue and bone that support the tooth. Resorption attacks the tooth itself, from the inside or at the neck, and is driven by the cat's own cells rather than by bacteria alone. The two very often occur together, which is why a full mouth assessment with radiographs matters more than a quick look.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-tooth-resorption/)
- **Q: How do I tell if my dog fainted or had a seizure?**  A: Fainting is a floppy collapse with a fast recovery, usually triggered by excitement or exertion, with no paddling and no loss of bladder control. A seizure typically involves stiffening, rhythmic paddling, jaw chattering, drooling, and a period of confusion afterwards that lasts minutes. Filming an episode is the single most useful thing you can do, because vets can usually tell the difference from a 20-second clip.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-fainting/)
- **Q: Is dog fainting an emergency?**  A: A single brief episode with a full recovery still deserves a same-day vet call. It becomes an emergency if the dog faints repeatedly, faints during exercise, has pale or blue gums, struggles to breathe, has a cough before collapsing, or does not come round within a minute. Those features point toward a serious cardiac or bleeding cause.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-fainting/)
- **Q: What causes a dog to faint suddenly?**  A: The most common causes are cardiac: arrhythmias, degenerative valve disease and cardiomyopathy. Cough-induced fainting, low blood sugar in toy puppies, anaemia, heat and exertion, and reflex vasovagal faints account for most of the rest. In older small breeds a heart murmur is often found at the same appointment.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-fainting/)
- **Q: Can a dog faint and be fine afterwards?**  A: Yes, and that is typical of syncope - the dog is normal again within seconds to a minute. Being fine afterwards does not mean nothing is wrong. Arrhythmias are intermittent by nature and often absent during a short examination, which is why ECG, Holter monitoring and echocardiography are used rather than a single listen with a stethoscope.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-fainting/)
- **Q: Can cats suddenly develop allergies?**  A: Yes. Allergies usually need repeated exposure before the immune system reacts, so a cat can eat the same food or live in the same house for years and then start itching. Onset often follows a move, a new pet, a diet change or a shift in season. Sudden intense itch with facial swelling or breathing difficulty is different and needs urgent care.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-skin-allergies/)
- **Q: How do I know if my cat's itching is fleas or food?**  A: Location is a clue but not proof. Flea allergy tends to concentrate at the base of the tail, lower back and hind legs, while food allergy more often affects the head, neck and ears. The reliable way to separate them is strict flea control on all pets for three months first, then a supervised eight to twelve week elimination diet, changing one thing at a time.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-skin-allergies/)
- **Q: Are grain-free cat foods good for allergies?**  A: No. Grains are rarely the culprit - animal proteins such as beef, chicken and fish cause most feline food allergies. A grain-free food often still contains the protein the cat already reacts to, so the itching continues and the diet change tells you nothing. A hydrolysed or novel protein diet prescribed by your vet is the meaningful test.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-skin-allergies/)
- **Q: Can I give my cat human antihistamines for itching?**  A: Not without asking your vet first. Several common human antihistamines and decongestants are toxic to cats, and the safe dose is nothing like a human dose. Cats also respond to antihistamines far less reliably than people or dogs do. Never use a dog flea product on a cat either - permethrin is a common cause of severe feline poisoning.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-skin-allergies/)
- **Q: Should I starve my dog with diarrhoea?**  A: A short 12 to 24 hour fast is often suggested for a healthy adult dog with a mild upset, but it is not mandatory and it is not appropriate for puppies, small breeds, seniors or dogs with other health conditions. Never withhold water. Most vets now prefer small bland meals over a long fast, because the gut recovers better with something gentle in it.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-diarrhoea-causes/)
- **Q: What can I feed a dog with diarrhoea?**  A: Plain cooked chicken or lean turkey with white rice, in four small meals a day, is the traditional home option. A prescription gastrointestinal diet is more complete and is the safer choice for puppies. Stop all table scraps, dairy, fatty treats and new chews while the gut settles, and keep the diet boring for three to five days after stools return to normal.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-diarrhoea-causes/)
- **Q: When is dog diarrhoea an emergency?**  A: Treat it as an emergency if there is blood in the stool - bright red or black and tarry - or repeated vomiting, a bloated or painful abdomen, a puppy under six months, an unvaccinated dog, a very flat or unresponsive dog, pale gums, or a suspected poison or swallowed object. Call your vet straight away in those cases rather than waiting for 48 hours.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-diarrhoea-causes/)
- **Q: Can I give my dog human anti-diarrhoea medicine?**  A: No, not without veterinary advice. Human anti-diarrhoea products contain ingredients that are not dosed for dogs and that can be harmful, and some contain opioids or salicylates. They also mask symptoms that your vet needs to see in order to work out the cause. Keep human medication away from dogs and ask your vet what is safe.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-diarrhoea-causes/)
- **Q: Can dog gingivitis go away on its own?**  A: Early gingivitis can improve, but not by itself. It needs plaque removed regularly, and brushing daily or at least three times a week is the realistic minimum. Leave the plaque undisturbed again for a few days and the gums become inflamed again. If tartar is already visible, brushing alone will not clear it and a professional clean is needed.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-gingivitis-home-care/)
- **Q: How can I tell gingivitis from periodontitis at home?**  A: You cannot tell reliably at home, which is exactly the point. Gingivitis is inflammation of the gum tissue, so you can see it. Periodontitis involves bone and ligament loss beneath the gum, which you cannot see. A vet needs a probe and dental radiographs. What you can track is the trend: worse breath, more bleeding, more tartar or reluctance to chew.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-gingivitis-home-care/)
- **Q: Is human toothpaste safe for dogs?**  A: No. Human toothpaste usually contains fluoride and sometimes xylitol, both of which are toxic to dogs, and the foaming action is hard to control in a dog's mouth. Use a dog-specific enzymatic toothpaste, which is formulated to be swallowed in small amounts. Human mouthwash is also not safe.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-gingivitis-home-care/)
- **Q: How often do dogs need a professional dental clean?**  A: There is no single schedule. Many dogs need one every 12 to 24 months, while small breeds with crowded teeth, or dogs that already have periodontal disease, may need an exam and assessment every six months. Your vet will set the interval based on what they find under the gum and on how good your home care is.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-gingivitis-home-care/)
- **Q: Why does my cat meow all night?**  A: Cats are naturally crepuscular - most active around dawn and dusk - so a quiet house at 4am is prime time for them. Beyond that, the usual causes are hunger from a single early-evening meal, boredom in an indoor cat with little to do, a closed bedroom door, a litter tray that is not clean enough, and - especially in cats over eight - a medical problem such as hyperthyroidism, kidney disease, high blood pressure or dental pain.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-meowing-at-night/)
- **Q: Is my older cat's night crying a sign of something serious?**  A: It can be. Sudden night calling in a cat over ten is a classic early clue to hyperthyroidism, chronic kidney disease, high blood pressure, failing eyesight, dental pain or cognitive dysfunction, and all of these are treatable or manageable. Book a vet visit rather than starting a training plan, and take a three-night log of when the calling happens and what else your cat is doing.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-meowing-at-night/)
- **Q: Should I ignore my cat when it meows at night?**  A: If your vet has ruled out medical causes and the behaviour is clearly demand-led, yes - completely. Any intermittent response, including talking through the door or getting up once to check, restarts the experiment from the beginning. Hold the line for one to two weeks while giving your cat a hard play session and a late meal, and most cats settle. Never punish with water sprays or shouting; it raises arousal and makes calling worse.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-meowing-at-night/)
- **Q: How do I get my cat to sleep through the night?**  A: Copy the natural hunt-eat-groom-sleep sequence: twenty minutes of intense wand-toy play, then a meal, close to your bedtime. Add a puzzle feeder for the small hours, more litter trays, a window perch, blackout curtains to blunt the dawn trigger, and a warm bed near a radiator. Cats respond to environment changes far more than to being told off.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-meowing-at-night/)
- **Q: How do I check my dog's body condition score at home?**  A: Use your hands as well as your eyes. Feel the ribs - they should be easy to find under a thin layer of fat but not visible. Look from above for a visible waist behind the ribcage, and from the side for a tucked-up belly line. Bones you have to search for or a waist that has vanished both mean excess fat. Most adult dogs sit at 4 or 5 out of 9.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-weight-check-at-home/)
- **Q: How can I weigh my dog without a vet scale?**  A: A standard bathroom scale works. Step on alone first and note your weight, then step on holding your dog and subtract. Small dogs can be weighed on kitchen scales, or held on a bathroom scale the same way. Weigh at the same time of day, ideally before breakfast, on the same scale, and repeat every two to four weeks so you have a trend rather than a single number.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-weight-check-at-home/)
- **Q: Is it normal for an older dog to lose weight?**  A: No - unexplained weight loss in an older dog always deserves a vet visit. It can point to dental pain, kidney or liver disease, an endocrine problem, inflammatory bowel disease or cancer. Loss of muscle along the spine and hindquarters without much change on the scale is also common after age seven and worth raising, because it affects mobility and is easier to slow if you catch it early.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-weight-check-at-home/)
- **Q: How much weight should my dog lose if it is overweight?**  A: Aim for a slow, steady loss with a vet guiding the target, rather than a crash diet. Start by cutting treats and table scraps, measure food with a kitchen scale or a proper measuring cup instead of guessing, and reduce the daily ration by around 10 per cent. Recheck the body condition score after a month. Rapid weight loss is not safe, particularly in small breeds, so get the rate set by your vet.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-weight-check-at-home/)
- **Q: How do I put eye drops in my dog's eyes without a struggle?**  A: Rest your dosing hand on your dog's head so your hand moves with them, pull the lower eyelid down to create a small pocket, and squeeze the drop into the pocket rather than at the eyeball. Warm the bottle in your hand first, keep the session under ten seconds, and give a treat within a second of the drop. Steady the head under the jaw - gripping the muzzle is what most dogs resist.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/how-to-give-eye-drops/)
- **Q: Can I use human eye drops on my dog or cat?**  A: No. Many human eye preparations contain ingredients that are unsuitable or unsafe for pets, and some - including preparations with certain preservatives or steroids - can worsen an eye problem that needs a different treatment. Only use drops prescribed for your pet, at the dose and frequency your vet specified.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/how-to-give-eye-drops/)
- **Q: What if I miss a dose of my pet's eye drops?**  A: Give it as soon as you remember, unless it is nearly time for the next dose, in which case skip the missed one and carry on with the normal schedule. Never double up to catch up. If you are missing doses often because your pet resists, tell your vet - a gel, an ointment or a long-acting preparation may suit you better than a twice-daily drop.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/how-to-give-eye-drops/)
- **Q: How long until eye drops start working?**  A: Squinting and light sensitivity usually improve within a day or two, discharge over a few days, and redness over several. The surface itself often takes longer to heal than the visible signs suggest, which is why you finish the course the vet prescribed. If there is no improvement at all after 24 hours, ring your vet rather than waiting.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/how-to-give-eye-drops/)
- **Q: Why is my cat losing hair in patches?**  A: Patchy loss is most often over-grooming from stress, fleas and flea allergy, ringworm or another parasite. Look closely at the skin: if it is red, scaly, crusty or broken, or the patch is spreading or itchy, that needs a vet visit rather than a change of shampoo. Take dated photos so you can show whether it is spreading.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-hair-loss/)
- **Q: Is symmetrical hair loss in cats serious?**  A: It deserves prompt attention. Hair that thins evenly on both sides of the body - flanks, belly or back - is more typical of an internal or hormonal cause such as a thyroid problem or Cushing's disease than of a skin infection. Bloodwork usually sorts it out, so book an appointment rather than waiting for it to grow back.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-hair-loss/)
- **Q: Can stress really make a cat lose its fur?**  A: Yes. Compulsive over-grooming is a common response to stress, a new pet, a moved litter tray or a change in routine. It typically produces a bald, smooth patch on the belly, inner thighs or flanks with short broken hairs. Reducing stress with more resources, more play and pheromone support helps, but check for medical causes first.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-hair-loss/)
- **Q: How do I check my cat for fleas properly?**  A: Use a fine flea comb over the lower back and tail base, then tip the debris onto a damp white tissue. Dark grit that turns reddish-brown is flea dirt, which means your cat has been bitten even if you never see a live flea. Treat every pet in the house with a veterinary product and continue for at least three months.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-hair-loss/)
- **Q: Does cat stomatitis go away on its own?**  A: Usually no. Chronic gingivostomatitis is driven by an over-reactive immune response to plaque, so it tends to persist or worsen without treatment. Some cats get partial control from regular dental cleaning and home care, but many need extraction of affected teeth or immune-modulating therapy prescribed by a vet.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-stomatitis/)
- **Q: What are the first signs of stomatitis in cats?**  A: The early signs are subtle: drooling, dropping food while eating, chewing on one side, refusing hard treats, much stronger breath, and a scruffy or greasy coat because grooming hurts. Some cats flinch or hiss when the face is touched. Cats hide mouth pain well, so any of these is worth a vet appointment.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-stomatitis/)
- **Q: Can I treat cat stomatitis at home?**  A: You can make your cat more comfortable by softening food with warm water, warming it slightly, using a shallow wide bowl and offering small frequent meals. You cannot treat the disease at home. Human painkillers including paracetamol, ibuprofen and aspirin are toxic to cats, so pain relief has to come from your vet.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-stomatitis/)
- **Q: Is it cruel to remove all of a cat's teeth?**  A: No - for cats with severe stomatitis it is often the kindest option. The pain comes from the inflamed tissue around the teeth, not the teeth themselves, and most cats eat wet and even dry food comfortably once their gums are no longer inflamed. Many owners report a dramatic improvement in mood and appetite afterwards.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-stomatitis/)
- **Q: How long is too long for a dog cough?**  A: A mild cough in a bright, eating dog often settles within one to two weeks. Anything lasting more than a few days, getting worse, or lasting beyond two weeks needs a vet visit. If the cough is wet, blood-tinged or comes with laboured breathing, fainting or a dog that will not eat, do not wait at all - book the same day.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-coughing-causes/)
- **Q: Can I give my dog human cough syrup?**  A: No. Many human cough medicines contain paracetamol, decongestants or other ingredients that are toxic to dogs, and dosing by owner guesswork causes real harm. Keep your dog comfortable with rest, a harness instead of a collar and clean air, and let your vet choose any medication.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-coughing-causes/)
- **Q: What does kennel cough sound like?**  A: Usually a harsh, honking cough that ends with a retch or a foamy spit, often worse after excitement, drinking or exercise. It spreads easily wherever dogs mix. Healthy adult dogs often recover with rest and supportive care, but puppies, seniors and unwell dogs should be seen because it can progress.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-coughing-causes/)
- **Q: Is a dog cough ever an emergency?**  A: Yes. A sudden, violent, repeated cough that started in one moment may mean an object or grass seed is stuck in the airway. Blue gums, gasping, fainting, collapse, or breathing that is fast and laboured at rest are also emergencies. Go straight to a vet rather than waiting to see if it settles.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-coughing-causes/)
- **Q: Can I train my cat to stop scratching the sofa completely?**  A: Not completely, because scratching is a core cat behaviour rather than a bad habit. What you can do is redirect it almost entirely in two to three weeks by placing an attractive, tall and stable scratcher beside the damaged furniture, protecting that furniture temporarily, and trimming the claws regularly. Most cats will keep one preferred scratching station, and the fight ends once that station is not your sofa.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-scratching-furniture/)
- **Q: Is declawing ever acceptable?**  A: It is a partial amputation: the last bone of each toe is removed along with the claw and tendon, and it can cause lasting pain, altered gait and behaviour problems. It is banned or restricted in many countries, and the AVMA advises it only as a last resort for a medical problem. Trimming, nail caps and proper scratching surfaces solve the same problem without surgery.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-scratching-furniture/)
- **Q: Why does my cat only scratch when I am in the room?**  A: Scratching is partly social marking, and some cats do it where the household gathers, often right after waking or when you come home. It is not spite. Give the cat a tall scratcher in that same room, ideally near where you sit, and reward the moment they use it so the marking happens on a surface you like.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-scratching-furniture/)
- **Q: Should I worry if my cat scratches itself instead of furniture?**  A: Yes. Scratching and chewing at its own skin, ears or face is a medical sign rather than a behaviour one. The usual causes are fleas, ear mites, a food or environmental allergy, or a painful claw or nail bed. Book a vet visit; no amount of behaviour work will fix itching, and this article cannot diagnose what is going on.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-scratching-furniture/)
- **Q: Is a watery eye in cats a sign they are sad?**  A: No. Cats do not produce emotional tears the way humans do. A watery eye means the tear film is overflowing the lid margin, which happens when the eye surface is irritated or the drainage duct to the nose is narrowed or blocked. Sadness or stress can contribute indirectly by suppressing the immune system and letting herpesvirus flare, but the tears themselves are a mechanical overflow, not an emotion.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-watery-eye/)
- **Q: How long can I safely watch a watery cat eye at home?**  A: About 24 hours, and only if the eye is wide open, the discharge is clear or very slightly sticky, and your cat is eating, playing and behaving normally. The moment you see squinting, the eye held shut, cloudiness, redness or yellow-green discharge, stop watching and book an appointment. A corneal ulcer can go from mild to serious inside a day.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-watery-eye/)
- **Q: Can I use human eye drops on my cat?**  A: Not without veterinary advice. Many human drops contain preservatives that sting and irritate a cat's cornea, and any product containing a steroid can make a corneal ulcer dramatically worse or let a herpesvirus infection run wild. Saline-only drops are less harmful but do nothing about the underlying cause. Clean the eye with warm water and let your vet choose any medication.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-watery-eye/)
- **Q: Why does the fur under my cat's eye look rusty brown?**  A: That is tear staining. The porphyrins in tears oxidise when they sit in the fur and leave a reddish-brown mark, and the constant moisture also encourages yeast. It usually means the tear duct is draining poorly rather than that the eye is infected, especially if the eye is wide open and comfortable. Keep the area dry, treat any underlying cause, and ask your vet whether a duct flush is worth doing.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-watery-eye/)
- **Q: At what age is a dog considered a senior?**  A: It depends on size. Small breeds under about 20 lb (9 kg) are usually considered senior from 8 to 10 years, medium breeds from about 7 to 8, large breeds from 6 to 7, and giant breeds from as early as 5 to 6. The practical takeaway is to move to twice-yearly check-ups and routine bloodwork once your dog passes that threshold, because large dogs age faster and develop problems earlier.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/senior-dog-care/)
- **Q: My dog is slower on walks. Is that just ageing?**  A: Usually not just ageing. Slowing down, stiffness after rest, hesitating on stairs and lagging behind on walks are the classic early signs of arthritis, which is very common in older dogs and very treatable. Weight control, joint-friendly flooring, adjusted exercise and pain relief from your vet can all help. Ask for a mobility assessment rather than accepting it as normal.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/senior-dog-care/)
- **Q: What tests should a senior dog have?**  A: A thorough physical examination with a weight and body condition score, a blood count and biochemistry panel covering kidneys, liver and blood sugar, a urinalysis, and blood pressure. Your vet may add a thyroid panel, chest X-rays, or an abdominal ultrasound depending on what they find and what you have noticed at home. Doing these every six months is what turns a problem from an emergency into a manageable condition.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/senior-dog-care/)
- **Q: How can I tell if my older dog is in pain?**  A: Look at movement and behaviour rather than sounds. Signs include stiffness when rising, reluctance on stairs or into the car, panting at rest, restlessness at night, a tucked tail, lip licking, eating more slowly, and being withdrawn or unusually clingy. Dogs rarely yelp with chronic pain. If you suspect pain, book an appointment - your vet can examine the joints and discuss options, and this article cannot assess your dog.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/senior-dog-care/)
- **Q: How common is food allergy in dogs, really?**  A: Less common than most owners assume. Food is thought to account for somewhere around 10 to 20 percent of allergic skin disease in dogs, with environmental allergens such as dust mites, pollens and moulds, plus fleas, taking most of the rest. It is still worth testing when the pattern fits - year-round itching, paws and ears, gut signs - but it should not be the first assumption.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-food-allergy-signs/)
- **Q: How long does an elimination diet take?**  A: Plan for 8 to 12 weeks of strict feeding with no other food at all. Skin needs weeks to settle, so judging at day 20 is the most common reason a trial fails. If the signs improve, your vet will usually have you re-challenge with the original diet to confirm the trigger - improvement alone is not proof.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-food-allergy-signs/)
- **Q: Are blood tests for dog food allergies accurate?**  A: Blood and saliva panels marketed for food allergy in dogs are not validated for diagnosis and produce a high rate of false results, which is why veterinary dermatologists rely on the elimination diet trial instead. An accurate panel would be convenient, but paying for an unreliable one often delays a real answer by months.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-food-allergy-signs/)
- **Q: Should I switch to a grain-free food?**  A: Not automatically. Grains are not the most common trigger - beef, dairy and chicken come up more often - and many grain-free diets still contain those proteins. A proper trial uses either a hydrolyzed prescription diet or a single novel protein chosen with your vet, not simply a grain-free bag from the shelf.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-food-allergy-signs/)
- **Q: How hot does a dog have to get before it is heatstroke?**  A: A normal dog runs about 101 to 102.5F. Heatstroke is generally defined as a temperature above roughly 104F (40C) caused by heat rather than infection, and the danger climbs steeply above 106F (41C). Because you cannot always tell the temperature by how the dog looks, the practical rule is simpler: heavy frantic panting plus wobbliness, red gums or confusion is an emergency regardless of the number.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/heatstroke-in-dogs/)
- **Q: Should I use ice or cold water to cool my dog down?**  A: Use room-temperature or cool tap water, not ice. Ice and ice-cold water constrict the surface blood vessels that are trying to release heat, and they add a shock risk in a dog whose circulation is already stressed. Wet the dog thoroughly, especially the neck, armpits, groin and belly, and get air moving over them with a fan or car vent. Then drive to the vet.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/heatstroke-in-dogs/)
- **Q: My dog seemed fine after 20 minutes in the shade. Do I still need a vet?**  A: Yes, at least a call. Heatstroke can cause delayed damage - abnormal clotting, kidney injury, gut damage - that does not show in behaviour on the day. A dog that cooled down quickly may still need bloodwork. Call your vet, describe the temperature, how long the exposure lasted and how the dog is acting, and follow their advice.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/heatstroke-in-dogs/)
- **Q: Can a dog get heatstroke just from sitting outside?**  A: Yes. Heatstroke does not require exercise. A flat-faced dog in direct sun on a humid 85F day, a thick-coated dog on hot pavement, or any dog in a parked car can overheat with no activity at all. Humidity matters as much as temperature, because panting stops working efficiently when the air is already saturated.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/heatstroke-in-dogs/)
- **Q: How often does a dog really need a professional dental cleaning?**  A: For a healthy mouth with good home care, every 12 to 24 months is typical, and some dogs stretch toward 3 years. Once there is established periodontal disease, extractions, a crowded toy-breed mouth or an inability to tolerate brushing at home, vets usually move to every 6 to 12 months. The stage of disease recorded on dental X-rays and the gum chart drives the schedule, not a fixed calendar.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/professional-dental-cleaning-frequency/)
- **Q: Is anaesthesia-free dental cleaning safe and effective?**  A: It is safe but limited. It removes visible tartar from the crowns of the teeth, which is cosmetic. It cannot scale or probe below the gumline, cannot take X-rays, and cannot treat the pockets where periodontal disease actually lives. The risk is false reassurance: teeth can look clean on top while bone loss continues underneath.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/professional-dental-cleaning-frequency/)
- **Q: Is anaesthesia risky for my dog?**  A: Modern anaesthesia carries a small but real risk, and pre-anaesthetic bloodwork, monitoring and the cuffed endotracheal tube exist to reduce it. For most dogs the risk of untreated periodontal disease - chronic infection, pain, tooth loss and effects on other organs - is the larger one. If you are worried, ask your vet to walk you through their protocol and the specific risk factors for your dog.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/professional-dental-cleaning-frequency/)
- **Q: What can I do at home to delay the next cleaning?**  A: Brush with an enzymatic pet toothpaste three to seven times a week, use only dental chews, diets or water additives with a recognised veterinary oral health claim, and check the gumline for redness and the gum margin for a brown tartar line. Home care does not replace professional cleaning, but good daily care can genuinely extend the interval between them.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/professional-dental-cleaning-frequency/)
- **Q: Is cherry eye painful for my dog?**  A: It is uncomfortable rather than severely painful in most cases - think of a dry, gritty, irritated eye. Many dogs are bright and eating normally but rub the face and squint occasionally. Because the exposed cornea can dry and ulcerate, any sudden squinting, cloudiness, thick discharge or constant pawing should be treated as urgent rather than routine.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-cherry-eye/)
- **Q: Will cherry eye go away on its own?**  A: Occasionally a very fresh, mild prolapse settles in the first few days, but you cannot predict which ones will and waiting carries a real risk of permanent dry eye. Have a vet assess it. If they decide to watch it, that becomes a decision made with the eye surface properly examined, not a guess.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-cherry-eye/)
- **Q: Can I just use drops instead of surgery?**  A: Drops treat the redness and keep the eye comfortable, but they do not put the gland back in place. If the gland stays prolapsed for months it can scar and stop producing tears, leaving lifelong dry eye. Surgical replacement is preferred over removing the gland for exactly that reason.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-cherry-eye/)
- **Q: Will the other eye get cherry eye too?**  A: It can. Cherry eye reflects an inherited weakness in the tissue holding the gland, so the second eye is at higher risk, sometimes within weeks and sometimes years later. Check both eyes daily for a while after treatment and mention any new redness or watering to your vet.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-cherry-eye/)
- **Q: How much water should a dog drink per day?**  A: A common guideline for a healthy adult dog is about 50 to 60 ml per kilogram of body weight, which is roughly one ounce per pound - so a 10 kg dog around 500 to 600 ml and a 30 kg dog around 1.5 to 1.8 litres. That total includes water from wet food, and it rises with heat, exercise and a dry-food diet.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/how-much-water-should-a-dog-drink/)
- **Q: Is it bad if my dog drinks a lot of water suddenly?**  A: A sudden, sustained increase in drinking deserves a vet visit. It can follow a change in diet, weather or medication, but it is also one of the earliest signs of diabetes, kidney disease and some hormonal conditions. Do not restrict the water - measure how much they drink and book an appointment.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/how-much-water-should-a-dog-drink/)
- **Q: How can I tell if my dog is dehydrated?**  A: Check the gums - they should be slick and wet, not tacky. Lift the skin between the shoulder blades; it should snap back instantly. Sunken-looking eyes, lethargy and refusing water are more serious signs. If two or more checks look wrong, treat it as a same-day vet visit.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/how-much-water-should-a-dog-drink/)
- **Q: Should I add water to my dog's dry food?**  A: Yes, it is a simple and safe way to raise total water intake, especially for dogs that eat kibble and drink little. A splash of warm water or low-sodium broth mixed into the meal works well. Introduce it gradually if your dog is fussy, and make sure the food is eaten within a short window rather than left out.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/how-much-water-should-a-dog-drink/)
- **Q: How often should I clean my cat's ears?**  A: For a healthy cat that grooms itself, once a month is plenty - and some need far less. Clean more often only if your vet has prescribed it for a condition such as an allergy or a mite infestation. Wiping daily when there is no debris strips the natural oils and irritates the skin.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/how-to-clean-cat-ears/)
- **Q: Can I use cotton buds or hydrogen peroxide?**  A: Neither. Cotton buds push debris deeper and risk perforating the eardrum, and hydrogen peroxide, alcohol and vinegar can damage the delicate lining of the canal. Use a veterinary cat ear cleaner and a soft cotton pad, and only on the parts of the ear you can actually see.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/how-to-clean-cat-ears/)
- **Q: My cat's ears have dark crumbly dirt - what is it?**  A: Dark brown debris that looks like coffee grounds is the classic appearance of ear mites, especially in a cat that shakes its head and scratches. It can also be a yeast infection or a bacterial one, and the treatments differ. Have your vet confirm what it is rather than treating blindly.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/how-to-clean-cat-ears/)
- **Q: Should I clean my cat's ears if they smell bad?**  A: A bad smell almost always means infection or an underlying allergy, and cleaning alone will not fix it. Have the ear examined first. A vet can check whether the eardrum is intact, which decides which products are safe, and prescribe treatment that addresses the cause.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/how-to-clean-cat-ears/)
- **Q: Why is my cat suddenly peeing outside the litter box?**  A: The two leading reasons are a medical problem - most often a bladder or kidney issue - and stress or a litter box problem such as a dirty box, a covered box, or another cat guarding access. A vet exam comes first to rule out illness, especially in male cats and seniors.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-peeing-outside-litter-box/)
- **Q: Is my cat peeing outside the box out of spite?**  A: No. Cats do not plan revenge. House soiling is a response to pain, an unpleasant box experience, or stress such as a new pet, a move or tension between cats. Treating it as spite and punishing the cat makes the behaviour more likely, not less.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-peeing-outside-litter-box/)
- **Q: How do I stop my cat from peeing on the carpet?**  A: Address the cause first - a vet exam, then the setup: one box per cat plus one, uncovered, unscented litter, in separate quiet places, scooped daily. Clean the spot with an enzymatic cat-urine cleaner rather than detergent, and block it temporarily with foil or a food bowl.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-peeing-outside-litter-box/)
- **Q: Is spraying the same as peeing outside the box?**  A: No, and the fixes differ. Peeing outside the box is usually a full squat on a horizontal surface and often points to a medical or box problem. Spraying is a small amount on a vertical surface with the tail quivering, and it is usually about territory and stress, most common in entire males.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-peeing-outside-litter-box/)
- **Q: Do I need to see a vet for a chipped dog tooth?**  A: Yes, get it looked at. A small enamel chip may only need smoothing and monitoring, but you cannot tell from the outside whether the dentine or the pulp is involved. A quick exam settles it, and if the pulp is exposed the clock is running on saving the tooth.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-broken-tooth/)
- **Q: My dog broke a tooth but seems fine. Can I wait?**  A: Dogs hide dental pain well, so seeming fine is not reassurance. If the pulp is exposed, the tooth will die and can abscess within days to weeks. Aim for a veterinary dental exam within 24 to 48 hours of finding a fracture, especially if you can see a pink, red or black centre.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-broken-tooth/)
- **Q: Will a broken tooth heal on its own?**  A: No. Enamel and dentine do not regrow, and an exposed pulp cannot heal itself. It becomes inflamed, then infected, and usually necrotic, which is why a fractured tooth needs treatment - a root canal to save it or an extraction to remove the source of pain and infection.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-broken-tooth/)
- **Q: Can I give my dog painkillers for a broken tooth?**  A: Not human ones. Ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin and paracetamol are toxic to dogs and can cause stomach ulcers or kidney damage. Call your vet, who can prescribe a dog-safe painkiller and book the dental exam at the same time.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-broken-tooth/)
- **Q: How long can a dog go without eating before it's a problem?**  A: A healthy adult dog can miss a meal or even a day without harm, and a fussy day with normal energy and drinking is usually nothing. Past 24 hours without food, or any refusal in a puppy, toy breed, senior or dog on medication, it stops being a waiting game and becomes a call to your vet.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-not-eating/)
- **Q: My dog won't eat but is still drinking and playful. Should I worry?**  A: Usually not on day one. Bright, drinking, toileting and active dogs that skip a single meal are typically just off their food. Watch the next two meals, keep the food warm and small, and call your vet if a full day passes or if any other sign appears.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-not-eating/)
- **Q: Should I change my dog's food if it stops eating?**  A: Not immediately, and never by swapping overnight. A sudden change is itself a common cause of a fussy or upset stomach. Try warming the current food or adding a little water first, and if you do change, mix old and new over 7 to 10 days.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-not-eating/)
- **Q: Can I give my dog something to boost its appetite?**  A: Only with veterinary guidance. Appetite stimulants prescribed by a vet are safe and useful once the cause is known, but using shop products or human medication to push a dog to eat can mask a serious problem and delay diagnosis.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-not-eating/)
- **Q: Is cat dandruff a sign of a serious illness?**  A: Usually not. Most flaking in healthy cats comes from dry indoor air, grooming gaps or diet. It becomes a medical flag when it appears with hair loss, scabs, redness, itching, black flea dirt, weight loss or a change in grooming behaviour - that is when a vet should look.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-dandruff/)
- **Q: Can I use human dandruff shampoo on my cat?**  A: No. Human anti-dandruff shampoos are formulated for a different skin pH and often contain salicylates, essential oils and perfumes that cats can absorb or lick off and react to. Use a cat-specific gentle or medicated shampoo chosen with your vet.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-dandruff/)
- **Q: How long does it take to fix dandruff in cats?**  A: If the cause is dry air, grooming or diet, expect visible improvement in two to four weeks with consistent humidity, brushing and omega-3 supplementation. If the coat looks the same or worse after a month, the cause is probably medical and needs checking.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-dandruff/)
- **Q: Why does my older cat have dandruff on its back?**  A: The back and tail base are the hardest places for a cat to reach. Stiffness or extra weight means those areas get less grooming, so dead skin builds up. It is worth a vet mobility check, because early arthritis is common and very manageable.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-dandruff/)
- **Q: Are ear mites contagious to other pets or to people?**  A: They are highly contagious between cats and dogs, and they spread through shared bedding and grooming tools, so every pet in the home should be treated simultaneously. Human infestation is rare and short-lived - usually a mild itchy rash - but the mites do not complete their life cycle on people.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-ear-mites/)
- **Q: Can I treat ear mites at home without a vet?**  A: Shop products rarely clear a full infestation because they miss the life cycle, and some over-the-counter products are unsafe for cats. Prescription treatment from your vet, applied to every pet in the house for three to four weeks, is the reliable route.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-ear-mites/)
- **Q: How long does it take to get rid of ear mites in cats?**  A: Expect the intense itching to ease within a few days and the debris to clear within one to two weeks, but you must continue treatment for three to four weeks to break the life cycle. Stopping early is the most common reason mites come back.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-ear-mites/)
- **Q: Why does my cat keep getting ear mites after treatment?**  A: Almost always because another pet in the home was not treated, or treatment stopped before the mite life cycle was finished. Bedding, brushes and carriers can also carry mites, so clean those at the same time as you re-treat every animal.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-ear-mites/)
- **Q: How long should I wait before calling the vet about vomiting?**  A: One isolated vomit in a bright, drinking, otherwise normal adult dog can be watched for a few hours. Three or more vomits in a day, anything lasting past 24 hours, or vomiting with lethargy, diarrhoea or refusal of water means calling your vet the same day rather than waiting.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-vomiting-causes/)
- **Q: My dog vomited once and then ate normally. Is that fine?**  A: Usually yes. A single episode followed by normal appetite, energy and drinking is typically dietary indiscretion and settles without treatment. Watch for repeats over the next 12 hours and keep the meal small and bland for a day.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-vomiting-causes/)
- **Q: Should I feed my dog after it vomits?**  A: Give the stomach a rest first - 6 to 12 hours without food in a healthy adult dog, with water always available. Then offer small, frequent bland meals. Puppies, small breeds and dogs on medication should be guided by your vet instead of fasted at home.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-vomiting-causes/)
- **Q: Is yellow foam in dog vomit serious?**  A: Yellow or white foam is usually bile from an empty stomach, common in dogs who have gone a long time between meals. It is not automatically serious, but repeated bile vomiting, or bile with blood, pain or lethargy, needs a vet visit.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-vomiting-causes/)
- **Q: Is brown discharge in the corner of my dog's eye an infection?**  A: Usually not. Brown or rust colour is often tear pigment (porphyrins) sitting on the fur, which is a grooming issue rather than an infection. Infection colours are yellow, green and pus-like, and typically come with redness, squinting or swelling.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-eye-discharge-colors/)
- **Q: Why is only one of my dog's eyes discharging?**  A: One-sided discharge is more suspicious than both eyes, because it usually points to a local cause: a foreign body, a scratch, an ulcer, or something trapped under the eyelid. That pattern is a same-day vet call rather than a home-care situation.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-eye-discharge-colors/)
- **Q: Can I use my own eye drops on my dog?**  A: No. Human redness-relief drops can mask serious damage and contain ingredients that are not appropriate for dogs. Use only a pet-specific eye wash for routine flushing, and let your vet choose any medicated drops.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-eye-discharge-colors/)
- **Q: How do I stop the discharge coming back every day?**  A: If it is clear or brown, keep the fur dry and trimmed, wipe gently two or three times a week, and ask your vet about tear drainage, allergies or eyelash problems. If it keeps returning in yellow or green, the underlying cause has not been treated and needs diagnosis.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-eye-discharge-colors/)
- **Q: My dog is still eating and wagging - could he really be in pain?**  A: Yes, very often. Appetite and tail wagging are not reliable pain tests, because dogs are wired to hide weakness. Watch for changes in movement, posture and sleep instead, and ask your vet for a pain check at the next visit.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-pain-signs/)
- **Q: Can I give my dog aspirin until I get an appointment?**  A: No. Human painkillers including aspirin, ibuprofen and acetaminophen can cause stomach ulcers, kidney damage or fatal toxicity in dogs, and they can interfere with what your vet needs to prescribe. Call your vet for advice on safe options.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-pain-signs/)
- **Q: My older dog is just slowing down. Is that normal aging or pain?**  A: Slowing down is common, but it should not be assumed to be untreatable. A large share of older dogs with stiffness have osteoarthritis that responds well to a proper pain plan. Book a mobility exam before you accept 'just old age'.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-pain-signs/)
- **Q: How do vets tell how much pain a dog is in?**  A: They combine your history with a hands-on exam, an assessment of gait and posture, and often imaging or bloodwork. No blood test measures pain directly, so your observations at home carry real diagnostic weight.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-pain-signs/)
- **Q: How often is it safe to bathe a smelly dog?**  A: For most healthy dogs, every 4 to 6 weeks is plenty, with waterless foam or wipes in between. Bathing more often than weekly strips the skin's oils and can cause a rebound greasy coat that smells worse. If you feel you must bathe weekly, the cause is likely medical.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/why-does-my-dog-smell/)
- **Q: Do dog deodorising sprays actually work?**  A: They mask odour for a few hours. On a dog with healthy skin and a muddy afternoon, that is fine. If a spray is the only way your dog smells acceptable, the underlying cause - ears, skin, teeth or glands - is still there and should be diagnosed.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/why-does-my-dog-smell/)
- **Q: My dog smells musty even after a bath. What is going on?**  A: A musty smell that survives a bath usually points to yeast in the ears or on the skin. Over-the-counter grooming will not clear it. Your vet can confirm with a swab or tape impression and prescribe the right treatment.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/why-does-my-dog-smell/)
- **Q: Is wet dog smell a sign of anything serious?**  A: On its own, no - it is bacteria and yeast in a damp undercoat. It becomes a flag when it lingers once the coat is fully dry, when the skin underneath is red or greasy, or when it appears in a dog who has never had it before.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/why-does-my-dog-smell/)
- **Q: Is a little cat breath normal?**  A: A faint odor right after eating is normal and fades. Breath that is strong, foul, or constant is not normal and usually means dental disease or another health issue worth a vet check.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-bad-breath-causes/)
- **Q: Can I just give my cat a breath mint or dental treat?**  A: Dental treats can help slow tartar in some cats, but they do not treat active disease, and human mints are unsafe. If the odor is persistent, a veterinary exam beats any over-the-counter fix.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-bad-breath-causes/)
- **Q: My cat eats fine but has bad breath. Is that okay?**  A: Cats hide pain extremely well and often keep eating with serious dental disease. Eating normally does not rule out a problem, so persistent odor alone is reason enough to book a check.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-bad-breath-causes/)
- **Q: How often should a cat have a dental cleaning?**  A: It depends on the cat's age, breed, and existing tartar, but many cats benefit from a vet-scored dental exam at least yearly, with professional cleanings as the vet recommends. Small and flat-faced breeds often need them sooner.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/cat-bad-breath-causes/)
- **Q: Can I put coconut oil on my dog's dry skin?**  A: A tiny amount is sometimes used, but many dogs lick it off or react to it, and it is not a treatment for the underlying cause. Skip essential oils entirely. Ask your vet for a safe, dog-specific product.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-dry-skin-causes/)
- **Q: How often should I bathe a dog with dry skin?**  A: Usually less often than you think, often every few weeks to a couple of months depending on coat type, using a gentle dog shampoo. Over-bathing makes dryness worse. Follow the coat-type guide above for a baseline.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-dry-skin-causes/)
- **Q: Will a better diet fix dry skin?**  A: If the cause is a fatty-acid gap, yes, a balanced diet or vet-approved supplement helps within a few weeks. If parasites, allergies, or illness are the cause, diet alone will not fix it, which is why a vet check matters.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-dry-skin-causes/)
- **Q: Is dry skin contagious to other pets or people?**  A: Simple dryness is not contagious. But some causes, like certain mites or ringworm, are, so a dog with patchy hair loss or spreading flakes should be checked before mingling with other pets.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-dry-skin-causes/)
- **Q: Should I comfort my dog during a storm?**  A: Yes, you can comfort, but keep it low-key. Normal, calm interaction is fine; frantic soothing or baby-talk can accidentally reward the fear. A safe space and your relaxed presence do more than words.  [read more](https://pet.goods-infinite.com/insights/dog-thunderstorm-anxiety/)
- **Q: Will my dog grow out of storm anxiety?**  A: Usually no, and it often gets worse without help. Early management and, when needed, veterinary or behavior support give the best outcome.
